history_of_present_illness: The disease is an acute endemic, noncontagious, but probably infectious febrile illness. It is characterized clinically by a continuous moderately high fever, severe arthritic and muscular pains, and a profuse, petechial eruption on the skin, appearing first on the ankles, wrists, and forehead and rapidly spreading to all parts of the body. The incubation period is 5 to 10 days, with an abrupt onset marked by rigors, headache, malaise, and severe pains of the larger joints without inflammatory changes. Some cases may have a prodromal period of malaise and chilly sensations. Hyperaesthesia and photophobia may be present. The eruption appears as macules from the second to fifth day, starting on the wrists and ankles, spreading over the extremities, and extending to the trunk, tending to become petechial. A toxaemic condition appears early, and a stuporous state is common, though the mind can remain clear. Constipation is a constant feature. In severe cases, icterus and vomiting tend to come on later. Gangrene of the tonsils, scrotum, and prepuce are noted, more commonly in the milder type seen in Idaho.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The disease is chiefly reported from certain sections of Montana and Idaho, with the two best known regions of prevalence being the Bitter Root Valley of Montana and the Snake River Valley of Idaho. It is also reported from limited sections of Washington, Oregon, California, Nevada, Utah, and is widely distributed in Wyoming. The virus, probably bacterial in nature, is transmitted solely by the tick, *Dermacentor andersoni* (*D. venustus*), which lives on domesticated animals. The arthropod host gets its infection from virus reservoirs found in ground squirrels, chipmunks, mountain rats, and other rodents. Ticks feeding on these rodents become infected and transmit the disease to man. Guinea pigs, white rats, and monkeys are also susceptible. The virus is transmitted by the salivary secretion of the tick, and an infected tick remains infective for the remainder of its life. Spotted fever is a disease of rural districts and tends to affect only one case per house, indicating a negative role for bedbugs or lice. It makes its appearance in the spring months when ticks are most abundant. The virus is present in the blood during the entire febrile course.
vitals: The pulse is not very rapid (90-110). The fever steadily rises day by day from an initial 102°F to reach a maximum of about 105°F by the end of a week or so.
physical_exam: The cadaver often shows marked jaundice with petechial spots on the extremities and trunk, marked venous engorgement, and dark, fluid blood. In the blood vessels, there is proliferation of endothelial cells leading to thrombosis. The lymph glands are enlarged. The spleen is three or four times its normal size, firm (unlike the soft spleen of typhoid fever), and microscopically shows extensive endothelial cell proliferation. The kidneys are enlarged and congested. Gangrene of the prepuce and scrotum are often noted, as well as gangrene of the tonsils in some cases. The characteristic skin eruption appears as macules, becoming petechial, first on the ankles, wrists, and forehead, then rapidly spreading to all parts of the body.
labs_and_diagnostics: Wolbach noted bacterial forms in the endothelial cells of guinea pigs infected with the virus, as well as in infected ticks. These include two morphological types: a chromatic-staining lanceolate diplococcoid organism found in circulating blood and endothelial cells, and a blue-staining rod-shaped form. Ricketts observed chromatin-staining bacteria, about 1 micron long by ⅓ micron broad, resembling *B. influenzae* and appearing as two lanceolate bodies, in man and in eggs of infected ticks; these are now considered part of the *Rickettsia* group. Wolbach named the organism *Dermacentroxenus rickettsi*. Frick found chromatin-staining bodies, often an elongated reddish body joined to a larger blue-staining protoplasm, within red cells of human cases and infected guinea pigs, as well as extracellularly. Ricketts proved the virus was not filterable. Early in the disease, there is leucocytosis, falling to about 10,000 after a few days, with an increase in large mononuclears and a decrease in eosinophile percentage. Albuminuria is an early sign of kidney involvement. A negative Widal test helps differentiate it from typhoid fever. Guinea pigs are susceptible to the infection and are more easily infected with Rocky Mountain spotted fever than with typhus fever.
differential_diagnosis: Typhoid fever (differentiated by more sudden onset, joint pains, and negative Widal test). Typhus fever (shows marked clinical resemblances; however, Rocky Mountain fever has a less abrupt onset and decline of fever, and guinea pigs are more easily infected with it). Tsutsugamushi. Trench fever.
management_and_clinical_course: The prognosis varies remarkably, with a mortality rate approximating 75-90% in western Montana, but only about 5% for Idaho. Prognosis is more unfavorable when nervous manifestations are marked. Death tends to occur in the second week, and patients surviving this week have a good chance for recovery. The death rate is greatest in old people and least in young children. Prophylaxis involves inspecting oneself for ticks after exposure, as *Dermacentor andersoni* requires at least one hour to attach and feed; removing ticks found can prevent infection. Ticks on grazing sheep have a high mortality rate (87%), possibly due to wool fat, and sheep can be dipped for further tick destruction. Treatment focuses on good nursing, similar to typhus fever. The patient's room should be darkened and quiet. Cool sponging helps lower temperature and acts as a tonic for nervous disorders. An ice cap can be used for headache. A liquid diet is recommended, and water should be given freely due to the tendency for renal involvement. Due to the tendency for heart failure, the recumbent position is demanded, and cardiac stimulants are indicated. Michie and Parsons found sodium citrate beneficial in infected guinea pigs and recommended it for humans, given intravenously at about 60 cc of a 5% solution twice daily. Immune sera tried by Ricketts showed no result.
final_diagnosis: Spotted Fever of the Rocky Mountains
